edges.description: Expressing the variant allele in a neuronal cell line is what produces the transcriptional signature, so the deletion acts on transcription in parallel with its effect on SH3 binding.

The characteristic facial features are modeled as a parallel consequence of the RBMX allele rather than a descendant of the brain-development branch; no source gives the developmental intermediates between the variant and craniofacial patterning. The allelic Shashi entry models its own facial gestalt the same way.

The ordering of these two molecular consequences is inferred rather than demonstrated. The only published link runs the other way as corroboration: EVPL, one of the significantly downregulated genes, itself encodes an SH3-domain protein, which the authors read as further support for reduced SH3 binding.

edges.description: Disturbed transcription during development is inferred to impair corticogenesis. The inference rests on RBMX loss-of-function models rather than on Pro162del patient brain tissue, which has not been studied.
Abnormal brain development produces the profound cognitive and psychomotor impairment that defines the syndrome.
Neuroimaging in an affected boy demonstrated a cortical malformation, the structural manifestation of the developmental defect.
The same MRI showed vermis hypotrophy, a further structural manifestation of the developmental defect.
The same MRI showed a thinner posterior corpus callosum, a further structural manifestation of the developmental defect.
Reduced brain growth is the direct anthropometric expression of impaired brain development.
Epileptic seizures are attributed to the abnormal cortical substrate; the specific epileptogenic intermediates have not been studied in this syndrome.
Spasticity reflects corticospinal involvement of the developmental brain lesion; the intermediates are not established.
Optic atrophy is placed with the neural and ocular consequences of RBMX loss; no work links the transcriptional defect to optic nerve degeneration specifically.
The severe hearing defect is modeled as a further neurosensory consequence, with unknown intermediates.
The defining cognitive outcome of the syndrome.
Restricted movement of the large joints accompanies the severe neuromotor impairment.
The severity of the neurological disease, with death commonly occurring during pulmonary infection, terminates in early childhood.
The optic atrophy is what carries vision loss to severe impairment or blindness in affected individuals.
Supports the requirement for rbmx in brain and eye development, the tissue-level node of this entry.
edges.limitations: This is a morpholino knockdown, not a knock-in of the Gustavson p.(Pro162del) allele, so it models loss of rbmx rather than the in-frame deletion, whose protein is still expressed at normal levels. Morphant phenotypes are also embryonic and global rather than a model of the human cortical malformation, and RBMX retrocopy buffering differs between species.

nodes.description: Characteristic facial features were reported as a family-level feature in the linkage study, and the 2023 report itemizes one patient's dysmorphic features (bitemporal narrowing, wide mouth, puffy eyelids, broad mouth, high palate). The binding stays at the general HPO term because the syndrome-level claim is the family-level gestalt; the itemized features are documented for a single patient and are deliberately not promoted to syndrome-level phenotype rows (see notes).

nodes.description: Residues 156-169 of hnRNP G bind SH3 domains in vitro, and deleting Pro162 weakens that binding about threefold for a short peptide against the BIN1-SH3 domain. The effect is context-dependent rather than absolute: a longer peptide spanning residues 150-170 showed no clear difference between wild type and mutant, and the natural cellular SH3-domain partners of hnRNP G are unknown. This node therefore records a credible but incompletely demonstrated molecular consequence, not an established pathway step.

nodes.description: RBMX function is required for normal brain development, and hemizygous RBMX variants produce neurodevelopmental disorders with variable brain malformations. In the Gustavson kindred the structural correlate is severe: neuroimaging in one affected boy showed lissencephaly with a very thick cortex. Zebrafish rbmx morphants lose forebrain and hindbrain marker expression and develop an underdeveloped head and eyes, supplying the developmental-biology basis for this node.

meta.association: Causal X-linked gene. The hemizygous in-frame deletion NM_002139.4; c.484_486del, p.(Pro162del) segregates with Gustavson syndrome in the Swedish kindred and is absent from public reference genomes. evidence.reference_title: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein G regulates splice site selection by binding to CC(A/C)-rich regions in pre-mRNA.
evidence.snippet: hnRNP G is part of the supraspliceosome, where it regulates alternative splice site selection in a concentration-dependent manner.

nodes.description: The initiating lesion is a hemizygous in-frame deletion of a single codon in RBMX (NM_002139.4; c.484_486del, p.(Pro162del)), which removes one proline from a tri-proline region of hnRNP G. The deleted base pairs lie in an evolutionarily conserved locus, and the variant is absent from public reference genomes. Because the deletion is in frame, hnRNP G is still produced: expression level and nuclear localization of the protein are unchanged in transfected neuronal cells, so the lesion acts by altering protein function rather than by abolishing the protein.
